title: Career roadmap · Product Designer (Digital)
summary: Build strong UX research, interaction design, visual design, prototyping, usability testing, design systems and product-thinking skills to design useful digital products from problem discovery through launch.

facts.Timeline assumption: This roadmap assumes a 4-year B.Des pathway from 2026–2030. Product design is portfolio-driven, so every academic year should produce at least one documented case study showing the problem, research, iterations, prototype, testing and final design.

horizons.question: What can I enter now?
horizons.output: Build UX fundamentals, visual design, interaction design, prototyping and usability-testing skills with 4–6 strong case studies.

horizons.question: How should I specialise?
horizons.output: Become a product/UX designer capable of owning features from discovery through delivery and working with product and engineering teams.

horizons.question: How should I evolve?
horizons.output: Move toward Senior Product Designer, Design Lead, design systems, product strategy or specialised product design.

horizons.question: How can I remain relevant?
horizons.output: Combine design leadership, product strategy, research, accessibility, AI-assisted design and business understanding.

blocks.text: 4-year honours variant

Use the additional year for a substantial product-design thesis, design research project, industry internship and a production-quality digital product. Document the entire design process rather than presenting only polished screens.
Specialisation options

Product designers should increasingly understand product strategy, analytics, accessibility, AI interaction patterns and design systems. AI can accelerate exploration and production, but strong designers still need to define the right problem, understand users, make trade-offs and validate solutions.

blocks.label: Portfolio tip
blocks.text: For product design, do not show only attractive screens. Each case study should explain problem → users → research → insights → alternatives → design decisions → prototype → testing → iteration → final outcome.

PhD routes
Possible research directions include:
A PhD is mainly useful for research, university teaching and advanced HCI/design research. It is not required for most product-design careers.

The strongest product designers will operate beyond screen design. Develop expertise in product strategy, user research, accessibility, design systems, experimentation, AI interaction, behavioural insights and business outcomes. AI will increasingly accelerate prototyping and visual production, so the valuable skill will be deciding what should be built, why it matters, how it should work and whether it actually improves the user's experience.
